draft.title: Bail and remand
card: Bail is the release of an accused person before their trial. It can come with conditions, such as reporting to police or living at a set address.
Remand is when a person is refused bail and is held in custody until their trial or sentencing hearing.
An accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty. This is why release before trial is often the starting point.
Bail laws also protect the community. A court looks at risks, such as the accused not turning up to court or committing another offence, and weighs them against the presumption of innocence.
draft.remember: Bail laws balance the presumption of innocence against community safety.

a.q: Which of these best describes a person on remand?
opts: An accused person refused bail and held in custody
An accused person released before trial with conditions
A convicted person released early from a prison term
An accused person found not guilty at trial
a.why: Remand means the court refused bail, so the accused stays in custody until the trial or sentencing hearing. Release with conditions is bail, which is the opposite of remand.
a.clue: Remand follows a refusal of bail.

b.q: A court in NSW refuses bail to Dan, who is charged with a serious offence and has failed to attend court before. Which reason best explains why bail laws allow this?
opts: They weigh the risk he will not appear against his release
They treat Dan as guilty because he has been charged
They punish Dan for the offence before the trial takes place
They end the presumption of innocence for accused people
b.why: Bail laws weigh the presumption of innocence against risks such as not appearing in court or reoffending. Refusing bail does not mean Dan is guilty or being punished, as he is still presumed innocent until proven guilty.
b.clue: Refusing bail is about risk, not a finding of guilt.
